Which meal tastes like a place to you?

Maybe it’s something you ate once, somewhere you’d never been before. Maybe it’s toast at your nan’s kitchen table. Food carries places, and the people we shared it with, better than almost anything.

Tell us yours in the comments: the dish, then the place. We’ll share a few on Sunday.

items.caption:
The best conversations start with a pause.

Not an awkward one. The small quiet after a question, when the other person is deciding how much to tell you. Leave it alone and the real answer usually arrives.

When did a pause change a conversation for you?

Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres. Inglés: Tell me who you spend time with, and I’ll tell you who you are.

It’s the Spanish cousin of “birds of a feather”. Half warning, half compliment, depending on who’s saying it.

Try it with a smile this week, when a friend starts sounding just like their flatmate: “Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.”

Who has shaped the way you talk? Tell us below.

Hoy recordamos contando historias. Inglés: Today, we remember by telling stories.

In Spain, 1 November is el Día de Todos los Santos, All Saints’ Day. Families take flowers to the cemetery, and bakeries fill with huesos de santo (little marzipan “saints’ bones”) and buñuelos de viento (light, airy fritters).

In Mexico, el Día de Muertos runs from 1 to 2 November. Families build an ofrenda, an altar with photos, marigolds and the favourite food of the people they miss, and tell their stories out loud.

Whose story would you tell today? Share it below, or tell someone at home.

A mal tiempo, buena cara. Inglés: Put a brave face on bad weather.

Very handy in a British November. It works for actual rain and for everything else: a cancelled train, a long week, a conversation that didn’t go to plan.

Try it the next time a friend’s having a rough day: “Venga, a mal tiempo, buena cara.” Come on, chin up.

What gets you through a grey week? Tell us below.

Word for word: whoever has a mouth gets things wrong. It’s what you say when someone mixes up a word and goes red. Nobody speaks without slipping, in any language, so say it anyway.

It’s the saying for week 19 of the Dime Más Journal: “Equivocarse forma parte de hablar.” Making mistakes is part of speaking.

Hello is where every conversation starts.

World Hello Day began in 1973, when two brothers, Brian and Michael McCormack, wrote to world leaders in seven languages about the importance of talking to each other. The idea is simple: say hello to at least ten people today.

The neighbour, the bus driver, the person you always nod to but never speak to. Who’s first?

Cada maestrillo tiene su librillo. Inglés: Everyone has their own way of doing things.

Word for word: every little teacher has their own little book. You’ll hear it when two people do the same job in completely different ways, and both get there.

The Dime Más Journal puts it like this: “Tu forma de aprender es la buena si te funciona.” Your way of learning is the right one if it works for you.
